newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin tax plan sparks dissent within Socialists.
newsitem.headline: Jospin tax plan sparks dissent within Socialists.

text.p: A leading member of Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's Socialist Party criticised the government ahead of the planned announcement on Monday of a deficit-cutting package which will fall heaviest on big business.

Left-winger Julien Dray told the conservative newspaper Le Figaro in an interview to be published on Monday that raising taxes on companies to put France back on track for a single European currency might jeopardise wage hikes.

"Taxing the companies is a dangerous exercise. If we inflict this on them today, you can bet that tomorrow, when we tackle the objective, which I think should be a priority, of boosting consumer demand with wage increases, the companies will retort that they are not milk cows."

"In addition, the freezing or the delay of a cut in Value Added Tax will prevent us supporting the hoped-for return of growth, at the risk of confining the French economy in the glum condition where it is now," Dray said.
Dray urged the government to discuss with Germany "our willingness to forge the Euro, but without giving up our political independence.
"This is not about having a deficit for the sake of it, nor about living beyond our means, but we must have efficient means to intervene in the face of our social difficulties," Dray said.

Jospin's plans will follow release of an audit of state finances showing that without corrective action France's 1997 deficit will significantly overshoot Maastricht treaty guidelines for qualifying for the European Union's single currency due to be launched in 1999.

Under the cuts, the corporate sector, not ordinary taxpayers, are expected to bear the load. Big companies, whose profits are at record highs, are likely to be slapped by a "euro surcharge" to raise 12 billion francs ($2 billion), sources say.

The government would extend into 1998 an "exceptional increase" in corporate tax to 40 percent of profits from the 36.6 percent. The companies could also be hit by a rise in the current 19 percent tax on capital gains on sales of assets.
But small and medium firms, seen as key to job creation in the battle to cut 12.5 percent unemployment, would be spared.
